doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Piano lessons, boogie woogie records and joining Gene Ammons
summary: Father's upright piano, Mance picking out melodies, his first teacher and the Tatum, Wilson, Hines records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well I was listening to an interview of yours on one of your records in “Jazzspeak,” and you were talking about how you learned from your father and —

In a sense, yeah. My father never played piano professionally. When I was oh I guess around five years old we moved to this apartment in Evanston, which is actually where I grew up, in the suburbs of Chicago. And whoever was there before us, just left this big old upright, you know, I mean big too. Uprights were like about six feet tall it seems like. It was probably too big and the person didn’t want to be bothered with moving it elsewhere. So my father had a good ear for music. He liked music. He listened, and he was very fond of big band music, like especially the Basie band. He thought there was no other band like the Basie band. And blues, my mother was more partial to blues. So my father was just fooling around on it, and he started taking lessons. Because by coincidence, the guy that lived down the stairs under us was a piano teacher. So he taught my father a few of the basics. You know my father would do it and I would just listen to him, and not even thinking about playing the piano. So when he was at work in the daytime, I would go to the piano with one finger and pick out these melodies you know. And one day he came home early and there I was. And he was listening. So you know when you’re a little kid you don’t know if you’ve messed up or what. So right away I says, “Dad, could I take piano lessons, I’d like to learn how to play piano.” And it floored him. Like what kid asks his parents if he wanted to take lessons? So he did, but he found me a better teacher than the one down the stairs. The guy down the stairs was more or less just taking people’s money, you know just teaching people that just wanted to know, you know making sense of these books, you know, learn how to play in five easy lessons. And so I went on from there. I really got to like it. And I had a great teacher. In fact my first piano teacher was the best of any teacher I ever had. He was, well he died a few

years ago, he was more or less a cocktail lounge type piano player. But the knowledge he had, his heroes, were like Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, Earl Hines in that order. You know so that was, those were the guys that I heard early in my career. And so what better three to listen to, to start off, you know, and he would play their records, you know like 78s back in those days you know, and they also put out these books of their solos, which some of them were impossible to read. I’m still not the greatest sight reader in the world you know, I’ve told the guys that. I read, but it’s more like spelling. But anyway, we went from that, and then my mother, liking the blues so much, she had all the boogie woogie records, like by Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons, Meade Lux Lewis, who also were living in Chicago then, those three. And ironically, I got my bebop chops from Albert Ammons’ son, Gene Ammons. I joined his band when I was seventeen.
